questions.q: Small text files a website stores in your browser to remember sessions and preferences are called:
questions.solution: Cookies hold site-specific data (login sessions, carts, preferences, tracking IDs). They are plain text files - not programs and not viruses.

questions.q: A cell displaying ######## (hash marks) indicates:
options: The column is too narrow to show the value
questions.solution: Excel fills the cell with # symbols when the formatted number cannot fit the column width - widen the column. It is a display condition, not an error.
questions.shortcut: Hashes = width, never an error code.

questions.q: Which utility shows running processes, CPU/RAM usage and startup programs in Windows?
questions.solution: Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc) displays processes, performance graphs, startup impact and lets you end tasks. Device Manager lists hardware/drivers; Disk Management handles partitions; Event Viewer logs system events.
questions.shortcut: Running apps + performance = Task Manager; hardware + drivers = Device Manager.

questions.q: A network confined to a single office building is classified as a:
questions.solution: A LAN (Local Area Network) covers a room, building or campus. MANs span cities, WANs span countries/continents.
questions.shortcut: Local = LAN; City = MAN; Wide/world = WAN.

questions.q: What does the phrase **cut corners** mean in the passage?
options: save time or money by skipping necessary steps
questions.solution: Context: codes cost money, drills take time, and officials want quick results. They are tempted to skip these costly steps — then 'the price of those saved rupees is paid in lives'. So 'cut corners' = do something cheaply or quickly by ignoring what is needed. The literal options are traps.
questions.shortcut: 'Saved rupees' in the next sentence confirms the meaning: saving money by skipping safety.
questions.passage:
Scientists who study earthquakes are frank about the limits of their craft. They can say which regions are prone to strong tremors and roughly how often such tremors occur, but they cannot yet predict the day or the hour. What they can do is reduce the toll. Buildings that follow earthquake codes sway without collapsing, and a school drill that teaches children to 'drop, cover and hold' can save lives in the first few seconds.

The trouble is that codes cost money and drills take time, while a big earthquake may not come for decades. Officials under pressure to show quick results are tempted to cut corners. When the ground finally shakes, the price of those saved rupees is paid in lives.

questions.q:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the highlighted segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select 'No substitution required'.

The child is very fond **of** his grandmother.
questions.solution: The fixed pair is **fond of** → the original is standard → No substitution required. 'Fond for', 'fond with' and 'fond at' are not English.
questions.shortcut: fond of — learn the pair; do not repair a correct sentence.

questions.q: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.solution: True drops its final e before -ly: **truly** (like duly). Truely keeps a phantom e; Truelly doubles an l that was never there.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes how the passage is organised?
options: A problem is stated, its causes are listed, and no solution is offered
A past decline is described, present-day advantages are given, and a practical obstacle to revival is pointed out
Two opposing views are presented and the author refuses to choose between them
A personal story is told first and general facts follow
questions.solution: Map: P1 — millets declined in the last century; P2 — their advantages today; P3 — the obstacle (no mills, low prices) and what is needed. The second option fails because P2 is about advantages, not causes, and P3 does suggest what is needed. There are no two opposing views, and the personal story comes last, not first.
questions.shortcut: Check every part of an organisation option against your paragraph map, in order. One wrong part kills it.
questions.passage:
For most of the last century, rice and wheat pushed millets off Indian plates. Government buying, cheap ration-shop grain and the prestige attached to 'white' cereals made coarse grains look like food for the poor. Farmers followed the market, and the area under jowar, bajra and ragi shrank steadily.

Millets, however, carry advantages that matter more today than they did fifty years ago. Most varieties need a fraction of the water that paddy demands and can survive on rain alone, which makes them a natural fit for dry districts where groundwater is falling. They are rich in fibre and minerals, and their slow release of sugar suits a population in which diabetes is rising.

Reviving them is not simply a matter of telling people to eat better. A farmer in Karnataka who switched part of her land to ragi found that the nearest mill was forty kilometres away and that traders offered her less than the support price. Unless processing units, storage and assured buying reach the villages, the campaign for millets will remain a slogan in city supermarkets rather than a change in what farmers grow.

questions.q: **Kathakali**, the dance-drama known for its elaborate green face make-up, is a classical dance of —
questions.solution: **Kathakali** is from **Kerala**; the poet Vallathol founded Kerala Kalamandalam (1930) to revive it. Karnataka's comparable dance-drama is Yakshagana (a folk form).

questions.q: DRDO test-fired the Long Range Land Attack Cruise Missile (LRLACM) in June 2026 from —
options: Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam Island, Odisha
questions.solution: The LRLACM was flight-tested on 15 June 2026 from **Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam Island (Wheeler Island), off the Odisha coast** — DRDO's dedicated missile-test island.
questions.shortcut: Missile tests → Abdul Kalam Island; space launches → Sriharikota.

questions.q: **National Science Day** is celebrated in India on —
questions.solution: **28 February** marks C.V. Raman's discovery of the **Raman effect** in 1928. 7 November is Raman's birthday; 11 May is National Technology Day (Pokhran-II, 1998); 15 September is Engineers' Day.
questions.shortcut: Science Day = discovery date, not birthday.

questions.q: The **tripartite struggle** among the Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas was fought for control over —
questions.solution: From the 8th to the 10th century the three powers fought for **Kannauj**, the symbol of supremacy over north India after Harsha.

questions.q: The incomes of A and B are in the ratio 9 : 7 and their expenditures in the ratio 4 : 3. If each saves ₹2,000, then A's income is:
questions.solution:
Incomes 9x, 7x; expenditures 4y, 3y.
$9x - 4y = 2000$ and $7x - 3y = 2000$ → subtract: $2x - y = 0$ → $y = 2x$.
Then $9x - 8x = 2000$ → x = 2000 → A's income $= ₹18{,}000$.

questions.q: From a point 20$\sqrt{3}$ m from the base of a building, the elevation of the top of the building is $30^\circ$ and of the top of the tower standing on it is $60^\circ$. The height of the tower is:
questions.solution:
Building: $h_b=20\sqrt3\tan30^\circ=20$ m.

Building + tower: $20\sqrt3\tan60^\circ=60$ m. Tower $=60-20=40$ m.

questions.q: What is the remainder when $1021 \times 1023 \times 1025$ is divided by 17?
questions.solution: $1020 = 17 \times 60$, so the remainders are 1, 3 and 5. Product $= 1 \times 3 \times 5 = 15$, which is less than 17. Remainder **15**.
questions.shortcut: Spot 1020 = 17 × 60 and write each number as 1020 + small.

questions.q: A starts a business with ₹30,000 and withdraws ₹10,000 after 8 months. B invests ₹20,000 for the whole year. The profit-sharing ratio is:
**Vikram walks 9 km towards South, then turns right and walks 12 km.** How far is he from the start?
questions.solution: Components (12, 9) = 3 × (4, 3) → distance = 3 × 5 = **15 km**.
questions.shortcut: 9-12 legs → 15 by the triple; no square root needed.
questions.pattern: shortest distance between start and finish

questions.q:
**Statement:** Out of the 60 employees of an office, 45 travel to work by metro.

**Conclusions:**
I. 75% of the employees travel to work by metro.
II. 15 employees travel to work by car.

Which of the conclusions follow(s) from the statement?
questions.solution: I: 45 ÷ 60 × 100 = 75% — **follows**. II: 15 employees do not use the metro, but they may walk, cycle or take a bus — 'by car' is not given — **does not follow**. Answer: **only I**.
questions.shortcut: The remainder is 'not metro', not any particular mode.

questions.q: **Amit's father is the only son of Ramesh.** How is **Ramesh related to Amit**?
questions.solution: 'The only son of Ramesh' is a child of Ramesh — he is Amit's father. So Ramesh → (Amit's father) → Amit: two arrows up, male → **grandfather**.
questions.shortcut: 'Only son of X' is simply X's child (male); decode it and the chain is short.

questions.q: If **+ means −**, **− means ×**, **× means ÷** and **÷ means +**, then what is the value of **48 × 6 + 3 − 2 ÷ 9**?
questions.solution: Rewrite: **48 ÷ 6 − 3 × 2 + 9**. BODMAS: 48 ÷ 6 = 8 and 3 × 2 = 6. Then 8 − 6 + 9 = **11**. (Left to right on the new line gives 19.)
questions.shortcut: Rewrite first; compute ÷ and × before − and +.
